short: Your own copy of somebody else's repository.
full: A fork lives under your GitHub account. You can change anything in it without affecting the original, which is why contributing always starts here — you are never editing the real project directly.

short: Downloading a repository onto your own computer.
full: git clone copies a repository from GitHub to your machine so you can open the files in an editor. You clone your fork, not the original.

short: A separate line of work inside a repository.
full: A branch lets you make changes without touching main. If the change turns out badly you delete the branch and nothing is lost. Every contribution should be on its own branch.

short: The default branch, holding the current good version.
full: Historically called master. This is what visitors see and what gets deployed, which is why changes arrive through pull requests rather than being committed to it directly.

short: A saved snapshot of your changes, with a message.
full: A commit records what changed and why. Small commits with clear messages are much easier to review than one enormous commit at the end.

short: Sending your commits from your computer up to GitHub.
full: Commits live only on your machine until you push them. git push -u origin your-branch sends the branch to your fork and sets it as the default target for future pushes.

short: A request to merge your branch into the original project.
full: Often shortened to PR. It is a conversation as much as a code change — maintainers read it, ask questions and may request changes before merging.

short: Combining your branch into another one.
full: When a maintainer merges your pull request, your commits become part of the project's history permanently, with your name on them.

short: Git cannot tell which of two changes to the same lines should win.
full: This happens when you and somebody else edited the same lines. Git marks both versions in the file and asks you to choose. It looks alarming and is genuinely routine.

short: A nickname for a repository somewhere else.
full: origin usually points at your fork and upstream at the original project. git remote -v shows what yours are set to.

short: The original repository you forked from.
full: Adding it as a remote lets you pull in work other people have merged since you forked, so your branch does not drift out of date.

short: A described piece of work, or a reported problem.
full: Issues are how projects say what needs doing. Ones labelled good first issue have been written specifically for people who have not contributed before.

short: A maintainer reading your pull request and responding.
full: A reviewer may approve, comment, or request changes. Requested changes are normal and are not a judgement of you — respond by pushing more commits to the same branch.

short: Somebody responsible for a project, who can merge changes.
full: Maintainers decide what goes in. They are usually volunteers, which is worth remembering when a reply takes a day or two.
